background.definition: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, a mostly asymptomatic bloodborne viral infection caused by a human flavivirus affecting the liver, is predominantly spread through exposure to blood or body fluids that contain HCV infected blood. HCV is a single stranded RNA virus that replicates primarily in hepatocytes without integrating into the host genome. HCV infection may present clinically as acute hepatitis, chronic hepatitis, chronic liver disease, cirrhosis or any of its complications including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and extrahepatic manifestations. Early diagnosis and treatment are key to avoiding severe liver damage, its complications, and prevent ongoing transmission.

list.listitem: The true incidence of acute HCV infection is difficult to determine as most acute cases are asymptomatic and under reported. In 2022, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimated 1.0 million new cases every year.

In 2022, the CDC reported a total of 4,848 acute HCV cases from 46 states, with an estimated 67,400 total acute HCV cases (incidence rate of 1.5/100,000 population) and 12,717 HCV-related deaths from 43 states in the United States. After yearly rises from 2015 to 2021, the reported cases of acute HCV decreased by 6.3% between 2021 and 2022. However, the rate has increased among non-Hispanic American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) persons by 7.4% (ie, 1.9 times as high as the rate among non-Hispanic White persons). Additionally, HCV-related deaths disproportionately affected non-Hispanic AI/AN persons (3.3 times) and non-Hispanic Black persons (1.7 times) compared to non-Hispanic White persons.
HCV is a global health problem, with worldwide variability in prevalence, with a global prevalence estimate of 1%. ,

In 2022, the WHO estimated that approximately 117 million people globally had serological evidence of HCV exposure, 50 million people worldwide (2.8% of the population) have chronic HCV and approximately 290,000 deaths per year from HCV secondary to cirrhosis and HCC. Only 36% knew their HCV status and only 12.5 million people (20%) got treatment for HCV. The highest burden of chronic HCV infection is in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (12 million people), followed by the Southeast Asia Region and the European Region (9 million each), the African Region (8 million), the Western Pacific Region (7 million), and the Region of the Americas (5 million). According to WHO about 2.3 million people (6.2%) of the estimated 37.7 million living with HIV globally have serological evidence of past or present HCV infection.
In the US, the estimated prevalence from 2017 to 2020 was 1.0% to 1.6%, corresponding to 2.4 to 4 million people with chronic HCV infection.

In 2022, CDC reported 93,805 new chronic HCV cases in 43 states, corresponding to a prevalence rate of 40.2 cases per 100,000 people, and highest among persons 30 to 39 years (80.2 cases per 100,000 population), among non-Hispanic AI/AN persons (104.8 cases per 100,000), and in rural areas (58.5 cases per 100,000).

The prevalence of genotypes varies globally and in many countries is unknown. In the US: 1a and 1b: 75% (1a>1b), 2 or 3: 15% to 20%, 4,5 or 6: <5%. Among the genotype 1 infections, genotype 1a is more common than genotype 1b.

HCV transmission among high-risk groups include those infected with HIV (17%-37%), IV drug users (52%), (2.3%-35%), hemodialysis (8%) homeless persons (27%-53%), prisoners (23%-41%), "baby-boomers" (born between 1950 and 1965) birth cohort (3.6%), those associated with surgery, dialysis, or transfusion (which are now rare in the United States), and non-injection drug users

In 2011, the total healthcare cost associated with HCV infection was $6.5 ($4.3-$8.2) billion in the US. Total cost is expected to peak in 2024 at $9.1 ($6.4-$13.3) billion. The lifetime cost of an individual infected in 2011 was estimated at $64,490 ($46,780-$73,190). When medical inflation was applied, the lifetime cost increased to $205,760 ($154,890-$486,890).

The National Hepatitis C Elimination Program is estimated to save $18.1 billion in direct healthcare spending, $13.3 billion of which will be federal savings. Over two decades, the health benefits would more than double and cost savings triple.

Treating HCV and preventing severe liver diseases such as cirrhosis and liver cancer account for most of the savings. Using the Hepatitis C State Policy Simulator tool can assist state health policy makers and practitioners to make informed decisions on screening and treatment policies. For example, the impact of adopting statewide universal HCV screening (10%/year) and unrestricted treatment (50%/year) by 2023 is estimated to prevent 1,200 deaths and yield $12.45 million cost savings, with an estimated cumulative per-patient HCV-related savings of $199,500 for end-stage liver disease.

Canada based retrospective study (2021), signified the economic burden to patient with chronic HCV. The out-of-pocket costs (OOP) for patient and caregiver time costs were assessed, based on reported total 3-month income for the hospital-based (14%) and community-based cohorts (21%), respectively. The community-based cohort had a mean 3-month OOP patient cost of $55, 3-month patient time cost of $743, 3-month caregiver time cost of $31. The hospital based cohort had a mean 3-month OOP patient cost of $299, 3-month patient time cost of $465 and 3-month caregiver time cost of $277. Costs were higher among the cohorts with decompensated cirrhosis.

Cost Savings with Treatment: Treating HCV can lead to substantial cost savings by preventing severe liver diseases such as cirrhosis and liver cancer. For example, the estimated cumulative per-patient HCV-related savings with treatment can be as high as $199,500 for end-stage liver disease. Treatment Costs: The cost of DAAs, the primary treatment for HCV, has decreased over the years. Initially, a 12-week treatment course could cost around $84,000 to $94,500, but prices have since dropped.

Based on Wong et all in 2021, chronic HCV in Canada a mean 30-day costs were noted to be $798 for no cirrhosis, $1487 for compensated cirrhosis, $3659 for decompensated cirrhosis, $4238 for HCC, $8753 for both decompensated cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, $4539 for liver transplantation, $11, 202 for terminal (liver-related) and $8801 for terminal (non–liver-related) health states. Comorbidity was the most significant predictor of total costs for all health states.

Iran based staudy (2015), calculated the estimated annual direct medical cost per patient at different stages of chronic HCV infection was an average $ 4591 ($614-$8574), with maximum cost for HCC and indirect cost $1054. The ratio of direct to indirect costs increases with the progress of the disease.

Cost-effectiveness among different countries on analysis of HCV screening showed significant benefits of screening in terms of its impact on morbidity and mortality in the local setting. Detection and treatment of HCV patients diminished HCV burden.

HCV-related mortality: According to the WHO 2024 Global Hepatitis Report, data from 187 countries the estimated number of deaths from viral hepatitis increased from 1.1 million in 2019 to 1.3 million in 2022, being the second leading infectious cause of death globally, of these 17% by hepatitis C. 3500 people/day are dying globally due to hepatitis B and C infections.

In 2022, CDC reported 12,717 HCV-related deaths from 43 states, with an age-adjusted death rate of 2.89 deaths per 100,000, a 9% decrease from 2021 (3.18 deaths per 100,000 people), and 43% decrease from the peak in 2013 (5.03 deaths per 100,000 population). HCV-related deaths are highest among persons 55 to 74 years, which accounts for 76% of all HCV-related deaths reported in 2022.

The death rates were higher among non-Hispanic AI/AN (9.08 deaths per 100,000 population), non-Hispanic Black persons (3.4 times (9.08 deaths per 100,000 population) and 1.7 times (4.75 deaths per 100,000 population), respectively) than among non-Hispanic White persons.The highest HCV-related death rate was reported in US Department of Health and Human Services Region 10.

Chronic HCV most common cause of chronic liver disease leading to cirrhosis, HCC and liver transplatation. HCC related to HCV is the fifth most common cancer worldwide, and linking approximately 85% to 90% of these cancers with HCV. Annual deaths per 100,000 population attributed to HCV, peaked in 2015 at 19,566 with steady decline to 14,242 in 2019, and 12,717 in 2022, worse among males versus females. Liver failure secondary to HCV infection a most frequent indication for liver transplantation in the United States.

A total of 12,717 HCV -related deaths were reported in 2022, with an age-adjusted mortality rate of 2.89 deaths per 100,000 population. highest among persons aged 55–74 years (76%), Non-Hispanic White persons accounted for 2.72 deaths per 100,000 population (64% ) and non-Hispanic Black persons (4.75 deaths per 100,000 population). Non-Hispanic Black person was 3.3 times and 1.7 times the rate among non-Hispanic White persons.
HCV is a small human flavivirus, an enveloped single stranded RNA virus that replicates primarily in hepatocytes without integrating into the host genome.

HCV causes both acute and chronic infection. New HCV infections are usually asymptomatic and clear spontaneously without any treatment depending on the age at the time of infection. About 50-70% may develop chronic HCV infection, with the risk of cirrhosis ranging between 15% and 30% by 10 - 20 years post infection and annual risk of HCC about 1-4%.

Acute HCV infection is based on one of the following: Clinically jaundice, peak elevated total bilirubin of >3.0 or peak elevated serum ALT >200 IU/L and the absence of a more likely diagnosis due to other causes or advanced liver disease OR by A Confirmatory laboratory positive test indicating presence of HCV antigen OR Positive HCV RNA test OR Presumptive laboratory positive test for antibodies to anti-HCV.

Acute HCV infection is mostly asymptomatic and is detectable by HCV RNA before antibody conversion. Spontaneous clearance of acute HCV infection occurs in 10% to 50% of patients within 12 months following an acute infection and 46% among MSM.

HCV has a high degree of genetic heterogeneity and seven major HCV genotypes with 67 subtypes are identified. Genotypes 1a, 1b, 2, and 3 are the most common genotypes in the United States. While the outcomes for each are the same, patients with genotypes 2 and 3 have a high likelihood of treatment response.
HCV transmits primarily through HCV infected blood products, body fluids and needles. Other less common modes are sexual and perinatal transmission.

The incubation period is 2-20 weeks after initial exposure to HCV, may be symtomatic or asymptomatic, self resolving or asymtomatic and progressing to chronic HCV. Overall 50-70% of people with acute HCV infection progress to chronic HCV.

The mechanisms of acute HCV infection progressing to chronic infection and liver injury are not well understood. Direct cytopathic effect of the virus and immune-mediated injury have both been implicated. Factors that are associated with viral clearance include: young age at diagnosis, female sex, presence of jaundice and IL28CC genotype.
The extrahepatic manifestations of HCV infection result from immune complex-mediated tissue injury.

HCV infection does not provide life long immunity against re-infection. Super-infection refers to a primary HCV infection followed by a secondary infection with a distinct HCV strain at a later point in time. Case reports have demonstrated that HCV can occur in humans including organ transplant recepients, people who receive multiple transfusions, or endoscopic examinations. Fluctuating or persistently elevated ALT levels and/or hepatitis flares may be observed, progressing to more severe liver disease.

WHO recommends that all adults have access to and be given HCV testing with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. No effective vaccine is currently available to prevent HCV infection. To end the global hepatitis C pandemic by 2030, WHO recommends decentralization, integration and task-sharing and POC HCV viral load assays and reflex viral load testing. Early diagnosis and treatment can cure over 95% of the infected people and prevent further transmission. C

WHO and USPSTF recommends one-time screening, opt out HCV testing, with anti–HCV antibody testing for all asymptomatic individuals aged 18 to 79 years, and during each pregnancy. If screening is positive and to confirm chronic infection and the need for treatment recommend a nucleic acid test for HCV RNA, a confirmatory PCR testing. B
One-time HCV testing should be performed for all persons less than 18 years old with activities, exposures, conditions or circumstances associated with an increased risk of HCV infection. C

Annual HCV testing and Periodic screening with anti–HCV antibody testing is warranted for persons who are at continued risk for HCV infection: infected with HIV, HBV, recipients of blood transfusions prior to 1992, persons with tattoos from unregulated parlors, persons who are born to an HCV-infected mother, and persons who have ongoing risk activities: injected drugs and shared needles, intranasal ilicit drugs, use of glass crack pipes, engagement in chem sex, long-term HD, and MSM, MSM taking PrEP. C
Improved infection control practices during medical procedures decreases transmission. C
Routine donor screening and product inactivation limits transmission from blood products, organs, and tissues Solid organ donors (living and deceased) and solid organ transplant recipients. A
Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B among HCV infected persons against pneumococcal infection with cirrhosis is strongly recommended. C

The USPSTF, CDC and WHO recommends one-time screening for HCV by testing for all asymptomatic persons aged 18 to 79 years in their life time. If HCV antibody screening is positive, follow-up or reflex testing using HCV RNA PCR should be performed. .
The WHO recommends decentralization, integration and task-sharing and POC HCV viral load assays and reflex HCV RNA testing, so all individuals have access to HCV testing.

In 2016, WHO declared an initiative to eliminate hepatitis C infection by the year 2030. The strategy proposed reducing new hepatitis infections, increasing access to testing and treatment, and improving surveillance and monitoring. Their target is a 90% reduction in chronic HCV incidence and a 65% reduction in HCV mortality by 2030.

WHO recommends periodic screening with anti–HCV antibody testing in places with high HCV antibody sero-prevalence in the general population (defined as >2% or >5% HCV antibody sero-prevalence), blood donor screening, persons who have continued risk for HCV infection: migrants from endemic regions, healthcare workers, sex workers, sharing needles or persons who inject drugs (PWID), on HD, and MSM; received clotting factor concentrates produced before 1987; have evidence of chronic liver disease; had a transfusion of blood or blood components or organ transplantation before July 1992; and all persons with HIV and/or HBV infection.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) 2021–2025 Viral Hepatitis National Strategic Plan for HCV elimination, for increasing the percentage of persons who have cleared HCV infection to at least 58% by 2025 and 80% by 2030.

CDC recommends (July 2023) testing for complete hepatitis C testing - HCV antibody test and HCV RNA testing in all adults, pregnant people, and people with risk factors to get tested for hepatitis C to eliminate the need for a separate follow-up appointment for HCV RNA testing.

CDC recommends to screen all infants and children 2-6 months old born to pregnant people with hepatitis C and detectable HCV RNA infants to be managed in coordination with a health care provider with expertise in pediatric hepatitis C.

Based on a recent systematic review of HCV screening and a RCT of screening among difficult to reach populations, combined strategies may be needed to impact screening among the undiagnosed. Health systems that choose to implement routine screening should be prepared to expand HCV treatment infrastructure; the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs accomplished this using nonphysician providers, telemedicine, and integrated care teams to address mental health and substance use comorbidities.

Consider screening for hepatocellular carcinoma at 3 to 6-month intervals using ultrasound or alpha-fetoprotein if ultrasound is unavailable for patients who achieve sustained viral response (SVR) following HCV treatment.

To reduce the risk of HCV infection: Practice universal precautions during medical procedures to reduce the risk of transmission Avoid sharing or reusing needles, syringes or any other equipment used to prepare and inject drugs, steroids, hormones, or other substances Harm reduction includes safe sex, and vigilant surveillance after viral clearance remain critical in reducing HCV transmission. practice of universal precaution.

In addition to treatment scale-up for acute HCV infection, limit transmission during high-risk activities and avoid using personal items that may have come into contact with an infected person’s blood, even in amounts too small to see, such as glucose monitors, razors, nail clippers, or toothbrushes
Counsel patients about risk reduction, frequent testing, and offer treatment of those infected and avoid getting tattoos or body piercings from an unlicensed facility or in an informal setting.
To minimize transmission from blood products, organs, and tissue, protocols should be in place to screen donors and to remove infected products from use..
Opioid substitution therapy, together with needle syringe programs, may decrease HCV transmission.

To date, two vaccine candidates have progressed to clinical trials in humans, but with limited success. One an adenoviral vector-based T-cell vaccine and the other a B-cell vaccine. Both have been unable to induce broadly neutralizing antibodies. Further research is ongoing regarding the HCV structure, and particularly the order of events following viral entry to the hepatocyte, where its membrane fusion process still remains poorly understood.Recently, a bivalent pangenotypic prophylactic vaccine with adenovirus vector encoding conserved sequences across HCV GT1-6 and modified HCV glycoprotein E2 has successfully induced both neutralizing antibodies and CD4+ CD8+ T-cell response in mice experiments. Further translational research is needed to confirm this candidate’s clinical efficacy.
Adopt primary prevention to prevent reinfection or co-infection.

Avoid alcohol and any new medication without prescription. To avoid transmission to others, avoid blood, semen, or tissue donation; avoid sharing personal items that may have blood on them; and cover any cuts or sores, Use barrier protection in case of multiple sexual partners.

Screen for HCV in patients infected for HIV and HBV. Vaccinate patients with chronic HCV infection against hepatitis A and B and for pneumococcal infection for patients with cirrhosis. For hepatitis A vaccination, recommend two-dose immunization against HAV or alternatively, a three-dose immunization combining hepatitis A/B can be used. For hepatitis B vaccination, typically the hepatitis B vaccine series consists of three doses using recombinant vaccine. However, a 2-dose hepatitis B vaccine series that can be completed in 1 month was similarly approved by the FDA.. C
Check anti-HCV antibody enzyme-linked immunoassay (EIA) and either follow-up or reflex testing with HCV RNA PCR to confirm the diagnosis. C

HCV RNA negative: no acute HCV infection. HCV RNA positive and HCV antibody negative: acute HCV infection. HCV RNA negative and HCV antibody positive: resolution of HCV infection. HCV antibody positive and HCV RNA positive: chronic HCV infection. HCV antibody positive and HCV RNA positive with six months prior HCV RNA negative and HCV antibody positive: reinfection of acute HCV. C

list.listitem: Acute HCV infection is usually asymptomatic. Based on CDC 2020 laboratory criteria for diagnosis of acute HCV in a patient >36 months of age (except known to have been exposed non-prenatally) include presence of one or more of the following: (1) jaundice, (2) peak elevated total bilirubin of >3.0, (3) peak elevated serum ALT >200 IU/L and the absence of a more likely diagnosis due to other causes or advanced liver disease due to previous chronic HCV infection or other causes like alcohol exposure, other viral hepatitis, hemochromatosis, etc and positive HCV RNA without antibodies to HCV.

Symptomatic acute HCV infection occurs in about 15% of persons. It is diagnosed in the setting of post-exposure surveillance, or sero-conversion in high-risk individuals (MSM living with HIV, healthcare professionals or injecting drug users) previously known to be sero-negative.

According to CDC 2020, chronic hepatitis C definition includes no available evidence of clinical and relevant laboratory information indicative of acute infections and a positive test for antibodies to HCV and hepatitis C virus detection tests with either nucleic acid testing for HCV RNA or HCV antigen positive test.

Acute HCV infection is rarely recognized due to the high rate of asymptomatic infections. If symptomatic, jaundice is the most common presenting symptom (65%-75%) followed by flu-like symptoms in 28% and abdominal pain/anorexia in 17% of patients.

Chronic hepatitis C also tends to be asymptomatic until the development of cirrhosis. The most common symptom is fatigue (62%), followed by itching (32%), abdominal pain (31%), dark urine (23%), and nausea (19%). Extra hepatic manifestations may arise in 40% to 75% of patients with chronic hepatitis C, and may be the presenting symptom ().

Thorough physical examination should include BMI, and searching for specific signs and symptoms that could orient towards the presence of complications of chronic HCV: ascites, caput Medusa, gynecomastia, jaundice, palmar erythema, splenomegaly, spider angiomata, and Terry’s nails.
Assess for any ongoing risk of HCV transmission: use of alcohol or any other substance use that may cause further hepatotoxicity, IV drug use, men who have sex with men, and barriers to treatment ).

Anti-HCV EIA is the first line test, with sensitivity and specificity about 99%. Assess quantitative HCV RNA viral load to determine whether the patient has chronic HCV, and to determine a pretreatment level. In the absence of treatment it is not necessary to repeatedly assess HCV RNA levels, as monitoring values over time does not provide useful prognostic information.

Recommended initial laboratory studies include CBC, thyroid studies, serum creatinine, hepatic function tests: AST, ALT, total and direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, serum albumin, and INR. Also obtain assays to detect relevant coinfections: hepatitis A antibodies, hepatitis B surface antigen, B core antibody, B surface antibody, and HIV antibody.

The qualitative HCV RNA PCR test can detect levels of > 50 IU/mL. It is 100% sensitive and 99% specific. It is used for diagnosis in sero-negative immunosuppressed patients with acute or chronic hepatitis, and for babies of HCV-infected mothers. Positive HCV RNA PCR determine infectiousness and to determine early response to treatment.

Persons found to have a positive HCV-antibody test and negative results for HCV RNA by PCR indicate no evidence of active HCV infection and are not protected from reinfection, universal primary prevention recommended. To distinguish between a true positive vs biologic false positivity, repeat testing with a different HCV-antibody assay for false positive HCV-antibody tests, that most commonly occur in populations with a low prevalence of HCV infection.

For persons with HCV exposure with a negative HCV-antibody test within the prior 6 months, perform baseline HCV-RNA, then follow-up HCV-antibody testing in 4 to 6 months or longer. HCV-RNA testing can also be considered for immunocompromised persons.
Point of care HCV testing for high-risk patients through the Genedrive HCV assay is available with 98.6% sensitivity and 100% specificity, now recommended by WHO.

Routine HCV genotype testing is not necessary for all cases, but is recommended for treatment regimen that are not pangenotypic. HCV genotype pretreatment testing aids in the selection of specific treatment regimen for those with evidence of cirrhosis and/or past unsuccessful HCV treatment.

Ultrasound (US) is highly specific in diagnosing compensated cirrhosis in chronic HCV patients. In a study of 1738 patients, it was 97% specific but only 34% sensitive. US is helpful when positive with a high positive predictive value, but not when negative.

The ratio of red blood cell distribution width (%) to platelet count (10^9/L) is a predictor of hepatic fibrosis. At a cutoff >0.17, it was 58% sensitive and 96% specific (LR+ 6.2, LR- 0.5). An AST/ALT ratio greater than 1, platelet count less than 140,000, or both increase the likelihood of cirrhosis or severe fibrosis/cirrhosis. Screening with ALT, AST, or GGT alone is not very sensitive for detection of hepatitis C or diagnosing cirrhosis complication.
Liver biopsy for patients with HCV prior to treatment initiation is currently not recommended.

Risk factors for HCC: (a) HCV individuals with high HCV RNA levels have a 14.7% prevalence of HCC compared to HCV RNA-negative (1.1%, p < 0.001); (b) 13.8% HCC if ALT ≥ 45 have compared to 1.7% if ALT < 15 IU/mL; (c) 12.6% with HCC if genotype 1 compared to 4.5% with other genotypes; (d) alcohol persists as a risk factor for all-cause mortality in patients with eradication of HCV post-SVR; (e) diabetes and fatty liver are independent risk factors for liver fibrosis progression and HCC in patients who have achieved SVR after direct acting antiviral therapy.
HCC incidence rate may be lower in patients who achieve SVR (5.1%) vs those who do not (21.8%).
Consider screening for hepatocellular carcinoma at 6-month intervals using ultrasound or alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) if ultrasound is unavailable for patients who achieve SVR.
A prediction rule can predict the likelihood of hepatocellular carcinoma, liver failure, and liver transplant in patients with chronic hepatitis C.
Prediction models are available to predict the likelihood of cirrhosis or severe fibrosis in patients with hepatitis C.

Hep C State Policy Simulator tool assists state health policy makers and practitioners to make informed decisions on screening and treatment policies. Eg: Impact adopting statewide universal HCV screening (10%/year) and unrestricted treatment (50%/year) by 2023 the cumulative impacts are 1,200 deaths prevented and $12.45 million cost savings.

Treat patients with HCV infection who are candidates for simplified regimen with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks, pangenotypic (irrespective of HCV genotype, any genotype). B

Recommended pre-treatment evaluation include complete blood count (CBC), glomerular filtration rate, (GFR), HBV, HIV, INR, and hepatic function panel (albumin, total and direct bilirubin, alanine transaminase, and aspartate aminotransferase). C
Response to treatment or SVR is confirmed by HCV RNA PCR concentrations below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ). A
Cure against HCV is achieved by sustained viral response (SVR). Pangenotypic direct acting antiviral (DAA) therapy regimens achieve about 95% SVR with 8 to 12 weeks of therapy. A
Liver transplantation is recommended for patients with decompensated liver disease. C
The AASLD and the IDSA in partnership maintain updated, evidence-based practice guidelines for the management of hepatitis C infection.

Goal of the treatment include eradication of the HCV, improving HCV related health outcomes and survival, and reducing the transmission of HCV to others. With DAA regimen, cure for HCV is more than 95%, in turn reduced prevalence of hepatic fibrosis, lower risk of developing hepatic failure, decreased occurrence of HCC, improved survival and improvement of some extra hepatic HCV-related manifestations.

Treatment is recommended for all patients with acute or chronic HCV infection, except those with a short life expectancy that cannot be remediated by HCV therapy, liver transplantation, or another directed therapy. Patients with a short life expectancy owing to liver disease should be managed in consultation with an expert.

Based on very low quality evidence, a cochrane review concluded that interferon-alpha may be effective in preventing patients with acute HCV infection from developing chronic HCV infection based on SVR measures. Effect of interferon-alpha on patient-oriented outcomes (eg, health-related quality of life, cirrhosis, decompensated liver disease, liver transplantation) remains uncertain. The authors were unable to find RCTs comparing DAAs with placebo or other treatments for patients with acute hepatitis C infection.

Approved DAA therapies for chronic hepatitis C infection include the following: ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni), glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Mavyret), ribavirin, sofosbuvir (Sovaldi), sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa), elbasvir/grazoprevir (Zepatier), and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir (Vosevi). Discontinued medications according to FDA include beceprevir, daclatasvir, ombitasvir/partitprevir/ritonavir, ombitasvir/pariprevir/ritonavir, and dasabuvir, simeprevir and telaprevir.

Factors that influence choice and duration of therapy include presence or absence of cirrhosis, medication cost, and insurance considerations. In cases where genotype 1 subtype is unknown, the individual should be considered HCV genotype 1a. In addition, drug interactions may also influence choice of therapy, particularly for individuals with HIV-coinfection.

Simplified treatment with a DAA regimen is recommended by AASLD/IDSA guidelines for patients with HCV infection of any genotype without cirrhosis in treatment naive adults. Persons diagnosed with acute HCV should promptly start HCV treatment. Initiation should not be delayed while determining whether spontaneous clearance of HCV has occurred. Reasons behind this decision relay on impact on reducing risk of transmission to others and risk of loss-to-followup after diagnosis.Recommended treatment is the same for acute or chronic HCV infection, and duration of therapy is also unchanged.

A Cochrane review found that while DAAs are effective in achieving SVR, there remains uncertainty in how DAAs affect longterm outcomes such as hepatitis C morbidity and mortality. Most included studies where short-term trials and the rates of morbidity and mortality were low.

Minimize exposure to other hepatotoxic agents, frequent testing, optimize medication adherence, and counsel and refer patients for treatment to minimize resumption of high-risk practices that could lead to reinfection. It is estimated that 25-35% of patients will spontaneously clear the infection; these individuals do not require treatment. Studies have shown that failure to clear the infection at 12 months after diagnosis is a risk factor for chronic infection.

This treatment is not eligible for patients with chronic HCV who have the following characteristics: prior hepatitis C treatment, cirrhosis, HIV and/or HBsAg positive, pregnancy, known or suspected hepatocellular carcinoma or prior liver transplantation.

listitem.strong: Simplified treatment in patients without cirrhosis

list.listitem: Per HCV guidelines HCV treatment for naive adults without cirrhosis must include assessment for eligibility: completing pre-treatment assessment that includes FIB-4 calculation, assessment for presence of cirrhosis, medication reconciliation, assessment of drug interactions and patient education. Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score helps to estimate the amount of scarring present in hepatic tissue, it is calculated by multiplying patient’s age in years by AST level in U/L, divided by platelet count (10.9/L) multiplied by the square root of ALT level in U/L. This can be obtained by multiple online calculators. Using a lower cutoff value of 1.45, a FIB-4 score <1.45 had a negative predictive value of 90% for advanced fibrosis. This is proposed by authors as a test that could potentially avoid liver biopsy with an accuracy for diagnosing liver fibrosis of 86%.

Laboratory tests to be requested, within 6 months of initiating treatment, include CBC, hepatic function panel, and calculation of eGFR. HCV viral load at baseline, HIV antibody/antigen test, and hepatitis B surface antigen must be tested prior to initiating treatment.

Recommended regimen for naive adults without cirrhosis per this simplified regimen describes glecaprevir (300mg)/pibrentasvir (120mg) to be taken with food for 8 weeks, or sofosbuvir (400mg)/velpatasvir (100mg) for a total of 12 weeks. Monitoring include: risk for hypoglycemia and anticoagulation status (monitoring INR). In-person or telemedicine visits may be scheduled for these purposes to provide, in addition, patient support, assessment of new symptoms and medication compliance. 12 weeks or after completion of regimen, HCV RNA and hepatic function tests are recommended to confirm virology cure, should HCV RNA be undetectable. In patients with elevated transaminases, after SVR is achieved, work up to look for other causes of liver disease is recommended.

Simplified treatment with a specific DAA regimen is recommended by AASLD/IDSA guidelines for HCV infection of any genotype in patients with compensated cirrhosis for treatment naive adults. Compensated cirrhosis is diagnosed based on any one of the following indicating cirrhosis: FIB-4 score >3.25, transient elastography or noninvasive serologic tests above proprietary cutoffs, clinical evidence of cirrhosis and platelet count <150,000/mm3, or prior liver biopsy showing cirrhosis. Simplified treatment for HCV infection is not appropriate for patients who have any of the following characteristics: current or prior episode of de-compensated cirrhosis, defined as Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) score ≥7 (ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, total bilirubin >2.0 mg/dL, albumin ≤3.5 g/dL, or INR ≥1.7); prior hepatitis C treatment; end-stage renal disease (ie, eGFR <30 mL/min/m2); HIV and/or HBsAg positive; current pregnancy; known or suspected hepatocellular carcinoma; or prior liver transplantation.

Regular laboratory monitoring is generally not required while on DAA treatment (a hepatic function panel is recommended at 8 and 12 weeks for patients taking elbasvir/grazoprevir). Warn diabetic patients to monitor for hypoglycemia and monitor INR for people taking warfarin.

Sustained virologic response (SVR): Gold standard for determining cure of HCV; quantitative HCV RNA [≤ 25 IU/ml] from an FDA-approved quantitative or qualitative NAT 12+ weeks following the conclusion therapy, and hepatic function panel normalization. If transaminases are elevated after achieving SVR assess for other causes of liver disease.

When SVR is achieved, despite detectable HCV antibodies, HCV RNA is no longer detectable in serum, liver tissue, or mononuclear cells, and substantial improvement in liver histology is achieved. This is considered virologic cure. Among persons who achieve SVR 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12), greater than 99% go on to achieve durable response and ongoing absence of detectable viremia. Long term follow-up of persons who achieve SVR12 or SVR14 has shown that nearly 100% remain RNA negative years after therapy. Several large studies have shown a minimal relapse rates of 0-1% in 5 years.

Serotype 1 without cirrhosis: In an RCT comparing 8 vs 12 weeks of therapy, patients given once daily glecaprevir/pirentasvir for 8 weeks had an SVR of 99.1% while those receiving it for 12 weeks had an SVR of 99.7%.

Serotype 3 without cirrhosis: In an RCT comparing 12 weeks of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir with sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, rates of SVR were 95% and 97% respectively. Previous DAA treatment failure: among patients with previous treatment failure with a DAA regimen (46% of whom had compensated cirrhosis), those randomized to sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir had a 96% SVR following 12 weeks of therapy.

Patients with renal impairment: An RCT of 104 patients with stage 4 or 5 chronic kidney disease (52% serotype 1, 16% serotype 2, 11% serotype 3, 19% serotype 4) found SVR in 98% following a 12 week course of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir.

Advanced cirrhosis: In a prospective international cohort of 530 patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis from HCV who received IFN-based therapy, sustained virological response was associated with lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 0.26; 95% CI, 0.14-0.49). However, there have been no long-term studies of the association between SVR and mortality in patients treated with IFN-free treatment regimens containing sofosbuvir and other DAA agents. A non-randomized trial found that non-hepatologist clinicians (primary care physicians and nurse practitioners) with additional training were able to successfully deliver hepatitis C therapy.
Liver transplantation is the treatment of choice for patients with decompensated liver disease.
Bile acids may improve liver function tests in patients with chronic HCV infection.
Alternative therapies including herbs and milk thistle have no proven efficacy.
Counsel patients to abstain from alcohol, illicit drugs, and any other hepatotoxic agents.

In patients with abnormal screening tests for alcohol use disorders, post-traumatic stress disorders, depression, and substance use disorder, integrated psychiatric and medical care resulted in rates of initiation and continuation of anti-HCV therapy comparable to those of unaffected patients getting usual care.
More than half of patients acutely infected with HCV will be chronically infected. B
Persons found to have a positive HCV-antibody test and negative results for HCV RNA by PCR indicate no evidence of active HCV infection and are not protected from reinfection. C
Progressive liver disease occurs in 15% to 20% of patients with chronic HCV infection; about 20-30% of patients develop cirrhosis over a 25-30 year period. B
About 1% to 4% of patients with HCV-related cirrhosis develop hepatocellular carcinoma each year. B

Once SVR is achieved for noncirrhotic patients, no liver-related follow-up is recommended. For patients with cirrhosis prior to DAA, ultrasound surveillance for HCC with or without alpha-fetoprotein testing is recommended every 6 months. C
Patients with HCV infection and diabetes appear to be at increased risk for HCC. Patients co-infected with HIV have higher viral loads and faster progression to chronic and severe liver disease. B

Follow-up for patients who achieve SVR or virologic cure: Once SVR is achieved for noncirrhotic patients, no liver-related follow-up is recommended. For patients with cirrhosis prior to DAA, ultrasound surveillance for HCC with or without alpha-fetoprotein testing is recommended every 6 months. Upper endoscopic surveillance for esophageal varices is also recommended. Patients with ongoing risk for HCV infection (eg, intravenous drug use or MSM engaging in unprotected sex) should be counseled about risk reduction, tested for HCV RNA and hepatic function annually, and counseled to avoid excess alcohol use.

Follow-up for patients who do not achieve SVR or virologic cure: Patients in whom initial HCV treatment fails to achieve SVR should be evaluated for re-treatment, and until re-treatment occurs, continue to be assessed for disease progression every 6 to 12 months with a hepatic function panel, CBC, and INR. Counseling to avoid excess alcohol use is also recommended.
Consider screening patients with HCV for hepatocellular carcinoma with ultrasound every 3-6 months and alpha-fetoprotein regardless of their SVR status in patients with advanced fibrosis.

All pregnant women should be screened for anti-HCV during each pregnancy, at the initiation of prenatal care, except in places where the prevalence of HCV infection is <0.1%. B Universal HCV screening implementation improved HCV detection and early management.

HCV-antibody–positive pregnant persons to assess the risk of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) and severity of liver disease screen with HCV RNA and liver function tests are recommended at initiation of prenatal care. No currently known intervention to reduce MTCT. Suspect intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) if pruritus or jaundice occur and assess for ALT, AST, and serum bile acids. B

Counsell all HCV-infected pregnant persons with cirrhosis about the increased risk of adverse maternal (ie, pre-eclampsia, cesarean section, hemorrhagic complication, and death) and perinatal (ie, preterm delivery, low birth weight (LBW), and neonatal death) outcomes. Their antenatal and perinatal care should be coordinated with a maternal-fetal medicine specialist. B
Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in women with HCV infection, except when the mother has cracked, damaged, or bleeding nipples, or in the context of HIV coinfection. B
Pregnancy does not negatively impact HCV infection. Women with HCV infection should have their HCV RNA reevaluated after delivery to assess for spontaneous clearance. B

HCV RNA levels can fluctuate during pregnancy and the postpartum period, rise during the first and third trimesters, reaching a peak during the third trimester, due to the release of tolerance in HCV-specific T lymphocyte responses that develop during pregnancy. During postpartum period slight decrease or spontaneous clearance of HCV were noted in studies up to 10% to 25% resolution rate due to the immunosuppressive effects of pregnancy and increased maternal plasma volume.

Risk of MTCT is believed to be increased if the maternal serum viral load is above 105 copies/ml. MTCT routes include intrauterine, intrapartum and postnatal. Elective cesarean section has not been proved to prevent transmission to the child. Surveillance published in the United States in 2017 revealed a nationwide increase in HCV infection among pregnant women.

MTCT of HCV has been estimated to occur in 5.8% of infants of HCV-RNA positive mothers who are not HIV positive, and 10.8% in HIV positive mothers. Risk of a HCV infected mother transmitting HCV to her infant is 4% to 8% per pregnancy, and 8% to 15% if co-infected with HIV and progress to chronic HCV 3-5%. No prophylaxis is available to protect the newborn from infection. HCV infection has no effect on pregnancy in the absence of de-compensated cirrhosis.

Prevalence of HCV among pregnant women is thought to be between 0.7% and 4.4%. There are limited studies that assess the effects of chronic HCV infection on maternal and fetal outcomes, however, a recent systematic review and meta-analysis reported an increased risk of preterm birth (OR 1.66 95% CI 1.59-1.74), IUGR (intrauterine growth restriction, OR 2.09, 95% CI 2.04-2.14), and LBW (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.63-2.36), compared to healthy pregnant women.

Other studies have linked HCV infection during pregnancy to increased risks of adverse perinatal outcomes eg: preterm delivery, LBW infants, congenital anomalies, ICP, anemia, increased cesarean-section rates and small head circumference, but worse with associated substance abuse.

Antiviral therapy is contraindicated in pregnancy to reduce MTCT due to the current lack of safety and efficacy data. However, on going studies are addressing potential options for treatment during pregnancy to decrease the risk of MTCT. Ongoing trials include a multi-center phase 4 study evaluating HCV treatment with sofosbuvir/velpatasvir during second and third trimester of pregnancy, as well as a phase I trial evaluating the pharmacokinetics of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir in pregnancy.

Current expert guidelines by the AASLD and IDDSA state that HCV "treatment can be considered during pregnancy on an individual basis after a patient-physician discussion about the potential risks and benefits".

Recommend screening for HCV antibody all infants born to HCV infected women. Screen infants for HCV antibody test, if reactive followed by anti-HCV RNA who are born to HCV infected women at 18 months of age or older who were not tested previously. If anti-HCV positive after 18 months of age, the infant should be tested with HCV RNA assay after age 3 years to confirm chronic HCV infection. If they were not tested already, for perinatally exposed infants and children up to 17 months, to be tested for HCV RNA test. A,,

Proper identification of perinatally infected children, referral to care, and curative treatment are critical to achieving the goal of hepatitis C elimination. Detectable HCV RNA infants to be managed by or with expertise in pediatric hepatitis C. A

Parents to be informed that HCV infected children do not pose a risk to other children, not transmitted by casual contact and, as such, can participate in school, sports, and athletic activities, and engage in all other regular childhood activities without restrictions. B

Parents should be informed that universal precautions should be followed at school and in the home of children with HCV infection. Educate families and children about the risk and routes of HCV transmission, and the techniques for avoiding blood exposure, such as avoiding the sharing of toothbrushes, razors, and nail clippers, and the use of gloves and dilute bleach to clean up blood. B

Prevalence of chronic HCV among children is 3.5 to 5 million worldwide. HCV infection in childhood is generally benign. About 25% to 50% of infected infants spontaneously resolve HCV infection (loss of previously detectable HCV RNA) by 4 years of age. Most infants infected with HCV at birth are asymptomatic, although severe liver disease can rarely occur. Approximately 3% to 8% perinatal transmision risk, being a common route for HCV infection among infants.

All cases under the age of 36 months are classified under perinatal HCV unless the exposure mode has been identified not to be perinatal (eg, healthcare provider, needle stick, blood transfusion, etc.)

There is no evidence that breastfeeding spreads hepatitis C. To discontinue breastfeeding if there is a cracked or bleeding nipple and to restart breastfeeding once healed, but not enough information is available regarding the risks of transmission. B
Consider routine liver function tests at initial diagnosis and annually to assess for disease progression. C
Vaccinations against hepatitis A and B are recommended early, along with other routine vaccines as per ACIP. C

Compared with adults, children are more likely to have asymptomatic infection, are more likely to clear the virus spontaneously, are more likely to have normal or near-normal aminotransferase levels, and have a slower rate of advancement to end-stage liver disease. Disease severity assessment by routine laboratory testing, physical examination, and noninvasive modalities (ie, elastography, imaging, or serum fibrosis markers) is recommended for all children with chronic HCV infection. Children with cirrhosis should undergo HCC surveillance and endoscopic surveillance for varices per standard recommendations. B

Use hepatotoxic drugs with caution in children with chronic HCV infection after assessment of potential risks versus benefits of treatment. Use of corticosteroids, cytotoxic chemotherapy, and/or therapeutic doses of acetaminophen, solid organ transplantation and bone marrow transplantation are not contraindicated in children with chronic HCV infection. C

Anticipatory guidance about the potential risks of ethanol for progression of liver disease is recommended for adolescents with chronic HCV infection and their families. Abstinence from alcohol and interventions to facilitate cessation of alcohol consumption, when appropriate, are advised for all persons with chronic HCV infection. C
Identify, follow, and treat HCV infected children. Children older than 3 years can be treated while those younger than 3 years are not eligible for therapy.

A systematic review of 4 RCTs and 31 non-randomized studies of PEG-IFN and ribavirin therapy in children with HCV found SVR rates that were similar to those in adults, and significantly higher in children with genotypes 2 and 3 compared to children with genotype 1.
HCV screening to be performed annually along with sexually transmitted infection screening. Acute hepatitis infection is asymptomatic common among MSM. C
To counsel about the risk of sexual HCV transmission with high-risk sexual and drug use practices, and educate about measures to prevent HCV infection or transmission. C
Initiate antiviral treatment for HCV-infected MSM, along with counseling about methods to reduce HCV reinfection risk of HCV reinfection. B
Annual HCV testing with HCV RNA is recommended for sexually active MSM after successful treatment or spontaneous clearance of HCV infection. C

HCV testing at HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) initiation and annually thereafter (while on PrEP) is recommended in HIV-uninfected MSM. PrEP can prevent sexual transmission of HIV, it is not protective against HCV or other sexually transmitted infection. Depending on sexual or drug use risk practices, frequent testing may be warranted. C

Since 2000, HCV infection among HIV-infected MSM have been reported. HCV incidence of 6.35/1000 person-years among HIV-infected MSM was reported in a systematic review (Jin, 2017). Group sex practices that can cause trauma to rectal mucosal tissue (ulcerative and rectal sexually transmitted infections including syphilis, lymphogranuloma venereum, genital herpes, receptive anal intercourse without a condom and receptive fisting) and rectal bleeding are determinats of HCV transmion.

High acute HCV infections among HIV-uninfected MSM who present for PrEP and who use of crystal methamphetamine, mephedrone, gamma-hydroxybutyrate and with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors before or during sex which lowers inhibitions, creates feelings of invulnerability, increases stamina, and inhibits ejaculation.

Among HIV infected MSM incident of HCV is higher due to increased rates of anal sex without condoms among HIV-infected men aim of minimizing HIV transmission risk. Among HIV/HCV coinfected MSM one-third shed HCV in their semen and rectal shedding of HCV are reported. High HCV reinfection rates, ranging from 7.3 to 15.2/100 person-years, have been reported after HCV treatment and cure among HIV-infected MSM.
